title: Refraction of Light
tagline: Learn laws of refraction, refractive index and applications like prisms and total internal reflection.

overview.intro: Refraction of light is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent medium to another due to change in speed. This chapter covers laws of refraction, refractive index, refraction through rectangular glass blocks and prisms, real and apparent depth, and total internal reflection with its applications. Ray diagrams, sign conventions for angles and correct use of Snell’s law are key for solving problems.

learn.title: Laws of Refraction and Refractive Index

blocks.text: When light travels obliquely from one transparent medium to another, it changes direction at the interface. This phenomenon is called refraction. The incident ray, refracted ray and normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane. According to Snell’s law, for a given pair of media, the ratio sin i / sin r is constant, where i is the angle of incidence and r is the angle of refraction.

The refractive index of a medium with respect to another indicates how much light bends and is related to the speed of light: n = c/v (absolute refractive index, relative to vacuum). Light bends towards the normal when entering an optically denser medium (slower speed) and away from the normal when entering a rarer medium.

items.text: Air to glass: ray bends towards the normal (r < i).
items.note: Glass is optically denser than air.

items.text: Glass to air: ray bends away from the normal (r > i).
items.note: Speed increases in the rarer medium.

learn.title: Refraction Through Glass Block and Prism

blocks.text: A ray passing through a rectangular glass block undergoes refraction at two parallel faces. The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced. The amount of lateral displacement depends on thickness of the block, angle of incidence and refractive index of glass.

A prism has non-parallel refracting surfaces, so an incident ray deviates towards the base of the prism. The angle between the incident ray direction and emergent ray direction is the angle of deviation. Deviation depends on angle of incidence, prism angle and material; for a given prism, minimum deviation occurs at a particular angle of incidence.

items: In a glass block, emergent ray is parallel to incident ray but shifted sideways.
In a prism, emergent ray is not parallel to incident ray.
Draw normals at each refracting surface to apply Snell’s law.
Use arrows to show direction of light in ray diagrams.

blocks.text: An object placed under water or glass appears raised when viewed from above due to refraction. The actual depth is called real depth, while the depth perceived by the observer is apparent depth. For viewing nearly normally from a rarer medium, refractive index n = real depth / apparent depth.

This effect explains why a pond looks shallower than it is and why a coin in water appears raised. The shift (apparent displacement) is real depth minus apparent depth. Accurate use of the formula requires identifying which medium is denser and which depth is measured.

items.meaning: Actual distance of an object below the surface of a medium.
Depth at which an object appears to be located due to refraction.
Sideways shift of an emergent ray relative to the incident ray in a glass block.

learn.title: Critical Angle and Total Internal Reflection

blocks.text: When light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal. As the angle of incidence increases, the angle of refraction increases until it becomes 90° at a particular angle of incidence called the critical angle (c). For angles of incidence greater than the critical angle, light is completely reflected back into the denser medium; this is total internal reflection (TIR).

Conditions for TIR are: light must travel from denser to rarer medium, and angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle. The relation between refractive index and critical angle (for denser medium relative to rarer, e.g. glass to air) is n = 1/sin c. TIR is used in optical fibres, prisms and mirage formation explanations.

blocks.caption: Applications of total internal reflection
rows: Small critical angle causes multiple TIR

blocks.text: Numerical problems may involve Snell’s law, refractive index from speeds, real/apparent depth and critical angle. Angles must be measured from the normal, not from the surface. When using n = sin i/sin r, ensure i and r correspond to the correct media pair and direction of travel.

Ray diagrams should show normals, correct bending at interfaces and arrows indicating ray direction. For TIR, show the ray striking the boundary at i > c and reflecting with angle of reflection equal to angle of incidence. Clear diagrams and labelled angles often carry marks in examinations.

items: Measure angles from the normal at the point of incidence.
Bend towards normal in denser medium, away in rarer medium.
TIR cannot occur when light goes from rarer to denser medium.
Use consistent refractive index convention as stated in the problem.

keyPoints: Refraction is bending of light due to change in speed between media.
Snell’s law: for a given pair of media, sin i/sin r is constant.
Light bends towards the normal in a denser medium and away in a rarer medium.
Refractive index relates to speed of light and degree of bending.
A glass block causes lateral displacement; a prism causes deviation.
Real depth/apparent depth equals refractive index for near-normal viewing.
Critical angle is the angle of incidence in denser medium giving refraction at 90°.
Total internal reflection occurs only from denser to rarer medium when i > c.
Optical fibres and totally reflecting prisms use TIR.
Angles must always be measured from the normal in calculations and diagrams.
examFocus: State laws of refraction and apply Snell’s law in numerical problems.

Define critical angle and state conditions for total internal reflection.
Explain applications of TIR such as optical fibres and prisms.
Label normals, angles and ray directions accurately.

questions.prompt: Refraction of light occurs due to change in its:
questions.answer: speed
questions.explanation: Light bends when it passes between media because its speed changes.
questions.commonMistake: Frequency of light remains unchanged during refraction.

questions.prompt: When light travels from air to glass, it bends:
questions.answer: towards the normal
questions.explanation: Glass is optically denser than air, so the refracted ray bends towards the normal.
questions.commonMistake: No bending occurs only for normal incidence.

questions.prompt: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from:
questions.answer: water to air
questions.explanation: TIR requires light to travel from a denser medium to a rarer medium at i > critical angle.
questions.commonMistake: The first condition for TIR is denser to rarer medium.

questions.prompt: For a given pair of media, sin i/sin r is:
questions.answer: constant
questions.explanation: Snell’s law states that sin i/sin r is constant for a given pair of media.
questions.commonMistake: The ratio of sines is constant, not the ratio of angles.

questions.prompt: The emergent ray from a rectangular glass block is:
questions.answer: parallel to incident ray
questions.explanation: Refraction at parallel faces produces an emergent ray parallel to the incident ray with lateral displacement.
questions.commonMistake: Parallel does not mean along the same line; there is sideways shift.

questions.prompt: The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which angle of refraction is 90° is called:
questions.answer: critical angle
questions.explanation: At the critical angle, the refracted ray grazes along the boundary (r = 90°).
questions.commonMistake: Critical angle is defined for denser to rarer travel.

questions.prompt: An object appears raised in water because of:
questions.answer: refraction
questions.explanation: Bending of light at the water-air surface makes the object appear at a shallower depth.
questions.commonMistake: Apparent depth is less than real depth for viewing from air.

questions.prompt: If refractive index of glass with respect to air is 1.5, the critical angle c satisfies:
questions.answer: sin c = 1/1.5
questions.explanation: For light going from glass to air, n = 1/sin c, so sin c = 1/n.
questions.commonMistake: Use the correct relation between refractive index and critical angle.

questions.prompt: The bending of light when it passes from one medium to another is called ________.
questions.answer: refraction
questions.explanation: Refraction occurs due to change in speed of light in different media.
questions.commonMistake: Reflection is bouncing back, not bending into another medium.

questions.prompt: For total internal reflection, the angle of incidence must be ________ than the critical angle.
questions.answer: greater
questions.explanation: When i > c and light travels from denser to rarer medium, TIR occurs.
questions.commonMistake: At i = c, refraction occurs along the boundary (r = 90°).

questions.prompt: The ratio real depth/apparent depth is equal to the ________ of the medium.
questions.answer: refractive index
questions.explanation: For near-normal viewing, refractive index = real depth/apparent depth.
questions.commonMistake: Ensure the correct pair of media is considered.

questions.prompt: State the two laws of refraction of light.
questions.answer: (1) The incident ray, refracted ray and normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane. (2) For a given pair of media, the ratio sin i/sin r is constant (Snell’s law).
questions.explanation: Both the plane condition and Snell’s law are required.
questions.commonMistake: Do not omit the first law about all rays lying in one plane.

questions.prompt: Define critical angle.
questions.answer: Critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°.
questions.explanation: It is defined only when light travels from denser to rarer medium.
questions.commonMistake: Specify that incidence is in the denser medium.

questions.prompt: State two conditions necessary for total internal reflection.
questions.answer: (1) Light must travel from an optically denser medium to an optically rarer medium. (2) The angle of incidence in the denser medium must be greater than the critical angle for the pair of media.
questions.explanation: Both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously for TIR.
questions.commonMistake: TIR cannot occur if either condition is missing.

questions.prompt: A pond appears shallower than its actual depth. Explain why.
questions.answer: Light rays from a point at the bottom of the pond travel from water (denser) to air (rarer) and bend away from the normal at the surface. When these refracted rays reach the eye, they appear to come from a point higher than the actual position. Hence the apparent depth is less than the real depth and the pond looks shallower.
questions.explanation: Refraction changes the apparent position of the object.
questions.commonMistake: Mention bending away from the normal when going from water to air.

questions.prompt: Draw and describe the path of a ray of light through a rectangular glass block, explaining lateral displacement.
questions.answer: When a ray of light enters a rectangular glass block obliquely from air, it bends towards the normal at the first surface because glass is denser. Inside the block it travels in a straight line and on emerging into air at the second parallel surface it bends away from the normal. The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways by a distance called lateral displacement. The displacement depends on the thickness of the block, angle of incidence and refractive index.
questions.explanation: Parallel faces produce equal and opposite bending in direction but a net sideways shift.
questions.commonMistake: Show normals at both surfaces and keep emergent ray parallel to incident ray.

questions.prompt: Explain total internal reflection in an optical fibre and state one advantage of using optical fibres.
questions.answer: An optical fibre consists of a core of optically denser material surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index. Light entering the fibre strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it undergoes total internal reflection repeatedly along the length of the fibre. This confines the light within the core and allows it to travel long distances with little loss. One advantage is efficient transmission of signals for communication with minimal energy loss and immunity to electromagnetic interference.
questions.explanation: Repeated TIR depends on the refractive index difference and incidence angle.
questions.commonMistake: State that the core must be optically denser than the cladding.

questions.prompt: A coin at the bottom of a water tank appears to be at a depth of 3 m when viewed from above. If the refractive index of water is 4/3, calculate the real depth of the coin.
questions.answer: Refractive index n = real depth / apparent depth. Given n = 4/3 and apparent depth = 3 m, real depth = n × apparent depth = (4/3) × 3 = 4 m. Therefore, the real depth of the coin is 4 m.
questions.explanation: Objects under water appear raised, so real depth is greater than apparent depth.
questions.commonMistake: Multiply apparent depth by refractive index; do not divide incorrectly.

questions.prompt: A ray of light passes from glass to air. Describe how the refracted ray behaves as the angle of incidence increases from 0° to beyond the critical angle.
questions.answer: At 0° incidence (along the normal), the ray passes straight without bending. As the angle of incidence increases, the ray refracts into air bending away from the normal, so the angle of refraction increases and remains greater than the angle of incidence. At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the boundary with angle of refraction 90°. For angles of incidence greater than the critical angle, no refraction occurs and the ray undergoes total internal reflection back into the glass.
questions.explanation: The progression shows refraction, grazing emergence and then TIR.
questions.commonMistake: TIR occurs only beyond the critical angle, not at it.

questions.prompt: Why does a totally reflecting prism often produce a brighter image than a plane mirror? Relate your answer to reflection of light.
questions.answer: A plane mirror reflects light by silvering, which can absorb some light and may deteriorate over time, reducing brightness. A totally reflecting prism uses total internal reflection at its internal surfaces, where nearly all incident light is reflected back into the denser medium without absorption by a coating. Therefore, the image formed by a totally reflecting prism is usually brighter and clearer.
questions.explanation: TIR provides almost complete reflection under suitable conditions.
questions.commonMistake: Base the answer on efficiency of reflection, not on refraction alone.

questions.prompt: Light travels from medium A to medium B and bends towards the normal. What can you infer about the optical densities and speeds of light in the two media? If the angle of incidence is 45° and angle of refraction is 30°, calculate sin i/sin r.
questions.answer: Bending towards the normal indicates that medium B is optically denser than medium A and the speed of light in medium B is less than in medium A. Using Snell’s law, sin i/sin r = sin 45°/sin 30° = (1/√2)/(1/2) = 2/√2 = √2 ≈ 1.414. This value is the refractive index of medium B with respect to medium A for the given pair.
questions.explanation: Direction of bending reveals relative optical density and speed.
questions.commonMistake: Use sine values of angles, not the angles themselves, in Snell’s law.

questions.prompt: State one similarity and one difference between refraction through a rectangular glass block and through a glass prism.
questions.answer: Similarity: In both cases, light undergoes refraction at two surfaces when passing from air into glass and out again. Difference: In a rectangular glass block the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray with lateral displacement, whereas in a prism the refracting surfaces are not parallel so the emergent ray is deviated and not parallel to the incident ray.
questions.explanation: The orientation of surfaces determines the relative directions of incident and emergent rays.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse lateral displacement in a block with angular deviation in a prism.
